data.name: Star Control®: Origins
data.detailed_description:
Explora uma galáxia repleta de civilizações alienígenas, novos mundos exóticos, combates emocionantes e uma história rica e cativante à espera de ser desvendada!

Parabéns! És o Capitão da primeira nave interestelar da Terra. Isso é ótimo. Espetacular. Até diria que é incrível. Só há um problema minúsculo. Se calhar nem vale a pena mencionar isso, mas uma raça alienígena hostil chamada Scryve está empenhada em exterminar-nos. Precisamos que recrutes aliados, descubras e uses as relíquias Precursor para melhorar a tua nave e evites ser devorado para conseguires salvar a humanidade. Mas não te sintas pressionado. É só o futuro da humanidade que depende de ti.

Caraterísticas:

  • Interage com alienígenas, tanto maliciosos como absurdos.
  • Explora um universo que transpira vida e está boquiaberto por te ver a navegar naquela... coisa.
  • Aventura-te por impressionantes mundos exóticos em busca de relíquias, artefactos Precursor e tesouros.
  • Viaja por milhares de planetas num universo com uma história cativante com centenas de milhares de anos.
  • Cria as tuas próprias naves ou transfere algumas do Steam para criar frotas e combater com elas nas batalhas de frota!
  • Cria ou transfere outros universos com a sua própria história, estrelas, planetas, alienígenas, naves e aventuras.
  • Mantém contacto direto com a equipa de desenvolvimento, partilha as tuas ideias e torna-te parte de algo espetacular!

Para de ler e junta-te a nós!

reviews.review:
8/10. A flawed-but-excellent successor to the original games. I was hesitant for a very long time about picking this game up, largely due to the mixed reception. I played a ton of The Ur-Quan Masters as a teenager, and so when I heard how different this game is I balked. That said, I’m glad I picked it up now that it’s more or less “finished,” and it seems like a lot of the non-fundamental criticisms have been addressed.

The most important thing to note about Origins is that it is NOT Star Control 2…2, which I think most of its detractors saw as its biggest issue. None of the original races return (except the Arilou in a very detached way), which to my understanding was the result of a protracted legal battle between the original SC developers and Stardock. However, many of the races clearly are designed to be at least spiritually similar to the classic races. The Tywom resemble the Spathi, being uncomfortably friendly and persuadable while also being fatalistic about their defenselessness and off-putting nature. The Drenkend resemble the Thraddash, being simple-minded bruisers. The Mukay are a combination of the Chenjesu and Orz - intelligent scientist squids that seem to frequently put themselves out of their depth (pun semi-intended). The Maelnir are similar to the Melnorme, enigmatic outsiders of the galaxy who are primarily interested in brokering information and exotic goods. And, of course, the Scryve stand in for the Ur-Quan Kzer Za as the hegemonic and oppressive empire that most of these races pay fealty to.

Gameplay is also similar, but done up since the original SC games. Combat still heavily draws from Spacewar!, using top-down combat with gravitational slingshotting around planets, wormholes, and energy/crew mechanics to balance the different ships and upgrades to your own vessel. It was never my favorite aspect of these games, but it feels much more fluid and accessible here compared to UQM. I would argue it feels a little too easy at times though. So far, I’ve been able to cheese my way through most encounters with the Shantid Destroyer by salvoing off plasma shots and running away. Encounters in general never feel too arbitrary or over-the-top, and so aggressors like the Kzanti Pirates  don’t reach the level of frustration that the Sylandro Probes do.

People also seem to dislike the planetary exploration, but it’s one of my favorite parts of the game! The lander was such a pain to control before, and things like lightning aren’t as arbitrary as they were in SC2. I’ve heard criticism about how planets are “gated” off without having access to heat and air filter upgrades, though you can access these pretty early on. It’s also simply fun to buzz across the surface while snagging fauna for the Malenir and dodging lightning strikes, wind storms, and volcanic boulders. Every planet has varying gravity and weather, which makes each expedition interesting as far as where and how quickly you can travel. Your lander cannon is also affected by gravity, so you can loft shots over hills and craters while avoiding return fire.

However, this is where I’ve run into most problems with the game itself. The lander is still awkward to control, frequently flipping over or getting wedged into small features. The sandworms are prone to glitching out and being stuck in a permanent chomping animation with no collision detection. I retrieved a drone that had a placeholder name instead of its actual one. The alien species and their animations are very limited, and so outside of hardly discernible color varieties you’ll be capturing the same 3-4 things on a planet. The planet scans also don’t seem to match what’s on the surface sometimes. It’ll describe a planet as “lifeless,” and then you’ll still find a few animals roaming the surface. Other times, it’ll say “Abundant,” which can mean anything from 8 to 25+ lifeforms. You’re generally only going to have one landing spot, as opposed to being able to pick anywhere like you could in SC2. This isn’t a HUGE issue, but it eliminates being able to smash and grab specific elements like you could before. However, landing no longer expends fuel, which makes repeat visits more worthwhile. This makes it sound like more bad than good, but these are still small nits for what is arguably the largest gameplay improvement over its precursor (pun intended). 

Speaking of, the writing and voice acting are excellent, but also a bit less open-ended and morally gray. Unfortunately, the Scryve aren’t nearly as complicated as the Ur-Quan. They lack the narrative depth of the Doctrinal Conflict and the real existential risk that the Kzer Za faces against the Kohr Ah, and how you’re really little more than a minor insurgency that they’d like to not bother with until it becomes evident you’re the only hope they could have of winning. The Scryve are more traditionally “evil,” but take notes from Ancient Rome on being an intellectually developed and overstretched empire in decline. The voice acting across the characters is emotive and professional, if not a little stereotype-laden. The Tywom all sound and act like Professor Zoidberg, Skyla with Star Control will scold you for making detours, and the Menkmack have voices and personalities to match their shrewd opportunism. Unfortunately, most minor races are unvoiced, but are written well enough to make up for it. The dry and dorky humor makes much of the game feel like a Star Trek analogue, and I think modernizes itself enough without sacrificing the series’ original charm. Animations for the dialogue screen are also fairly well-done for a game from around this time. It’s still fairly evocative of Bethsoft RPGs where mouths mostly flap in sync with the words, but the movement and body language in the dialogue and battle windows add a degree of expressiveness that make it far more engaging.

Overall, I think Origins fairs well as a modernization of the series while keeping most of its spirit intact. It makes for a much stronger 3D follow-up than SC3, which had good intentions but made weird design decisions (puppets) that syphoned a lot of the appeal away from UQM. It’s a very imperfect game, and I wish Stardock would push more bugfixes to address these minor issues, but for the price and amount of content presented, it makes for a great pickup alongside the “true” SC2 sequel, Children of Infinity, once it finally releases.
